stem: A nurse is caring for a client at 16 weeks gestation who is scheduled for an amniocentesis. Which nursing action is the priority before the procedure?

options.text: Instruct the client to empty her bladder
Verify the client's Rh status and blood type
Administer a sedative as prescribed
Position the client in left lateral position

rationale: Before amniocentesis, verifying Rh status is the priority because an Rh-negative mother may need RhoGAM (Rh immunoglobulin) after the procedure to prevent Rh sensitization from fetal blood mixing. The client should have a full bladder before 20 weeks (to support the uterus) and empty it after 20 weeks. Sedation is not routinely required. The client is positioned supine, not lateral, during the procedure. Source: Nurseslabs — Amniocentesis Nursing Responsibilities; RegisteredNurseRN — Prenatal Testing Review.

stem: A nurse is providing pre-procedure education to a client scheduled for a colonoscopy. Which instruction should the nurse include?

options.text: "You will need to follow a clear liquid diet for 1 to 2 days before the procedure"
"You may eat a regular breakfast on the morning of the procedure"
"You should take your aspirin as usual the morning of the exam"
"The procedure does not require any bowel preparation"

rationale: Colonoscopy requires thorough bowel preparation including a clear liquid diet for 1-2 days before the procedure and a prescribed bowel prep solution. The client must be NPO after midnight. Aspirin and other anticoagulants are typically held 5-7 days before the procedure due to biopsy/polypectomy risk. Adequate bowel preparation is essential for proper visualization. Source: Nurseslabs — Colonoscopy Nursing Care; RNpedia — GI Diagnostic Procedures.

stem: A nurse is screening a client prior to an MRI. Which finding would require the nurse to notify the radiologist before proceeding?

options.text: The client has a titanium hip replacement
The client has a cardiac pacemaker
The client is wearing a cotton hospital gown
The client has a history of latex allergy

rationale: A cardiac pacemaker is an absolute contraindication for MRI because the strong magnetic field can cause the device to malfunction, overheat, or move, potentially causing life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias. Titanium implants are generally MRI-safe as titanium is non-ferromagnetic. Cotton gowns have no metal components. Latex allergy is not an MRI contraindication. Other MRI contraindications include cochlear implants, metallic foreign bodies, and some aneurysm clips. Source: Nurseslabs — MRI Nursing Care; RegisteredNurseRN — Diagnostic Procedures.

stem: A nurse is preparing a client for a bone marrow biopsy from the posterior iliac crest. Which position should the nurse assist the client into for the procedure?

options.text: Supine with knees flexed
Prone or lateral with knees drawn to chest
High Fowler's position
Lithotomy position

rationale: For a bone marrow biopsy from the posterior iliac crest, the client is positioned prone or in the lateral (side-lying) position with knees drawn to the chest to expose the posterior iliac crest. Post-procedure, the client should lie on the biopsy site for 30-60 minutes to apply pressure and prevent bleeding. The nurse should monitor for bleeding, infection, and pain at the site. Source: Nurseslabs — Bone Marrow Biopsy; Naxlex — Hematologic Procedures.

stem: A nurse is interpreting a client's ECG rhythm strip. The strip shows a regular rhythm, a rate of 72 bpm, P waves present before each QRS complex, a PR interval of 0.18 seconds, and a QRS duration of 0.08 seconds. Which conclusions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: The rhythm is normal sinus rhythm
The PR interval is within normal limits
The QRS complex duration indicates a bundle branch block
The heart rate is bradycardic
The QRS complex duration is within normal limits

rationale: This ECG shows normal sinus rhythm (NSR): regular rhythm, rate 60-100 bpm, P wave before each QRS, PR interval 0.12-0.20 sec, and QRS duration <0.12 sec. The PR interval of 0.18 sec is normal (0.12-0.20 sec). The QRS of 0.08 sec is normal (<0.12 sec) — a bundle branch block would show QRS >0.12 sec. The rate of 72 bpm is normal, not bradycardic (bradycardia is <60 bpm). Source: RegisteredNurseRN — ECG Interpretation; Nurseslabs — Cardiac Rhythm Interpretation.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client who had a lumbar puncture 2 hours ago. The client reports a severe headache. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Elevate the head of the bed to 45 degrees
Encourage the client to remain flat in bed and increase fluid intake
Apply an ice pack to the puncture site
Immediately notify the provider for an emergency CT scan

rationale: Post-lumbar puncture headache (spinal headache) occurs due to CSF leakage from the puncture site. The priority nursing intervention is to keep the client flat (supine) for 4-8 hours and encourage increased fluid intake (oral and IV) to promote CSF production and replacement. Elevating the head would worsen the headache by increasing CSF drainage. An ice pack does not address the cause. While the provider should be informed, a spinal headache is an expected complication and does not require an emergency CT scan. Source: Nurseslabs — Lumbar Puncture Nursing Care; RegisteredNurseRN — Neurological Procedures.

stem: A nurse is reviewing the comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) results of a client. Which result should the nurse report to the healthcare provider immediately?

options.text: Sodium 140 mEq/L
Potassium 6.2 mEq/L
Glucose 95 mg/dL
BUN 18 mg/dL

rationale: A potassium level of 6.2 mEq/L is critically elevated (normal: 3.5-5.0 mEq/L) and requires immediate reporting because hyperkalemia can cause life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias, including ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest. ECG changes (peaked T waves, widened QRS) may occur. Sodium 140 mEq/L (normal: 136-145), glucose 95 mg/dL (normal fasting: 70-100), and BUN 18 mg/dL (normal: 7-20) are all within normal limits. Source: RegisteredNurseRN — Lab Values NCLEX Review; Nurseslabs — CMP Interpretation.

stem: A nurse is reviewing the complete blood count (CBC) of a client receiving chemotherapy. Which result indicates the client is at highest risk for infection and requires protective precautions?

options.text: Hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL
Platelet count 140,000/mm³
White blood cell count 1,500/mm³
Hematocrit 36%

rationale: A WBC count of 1,500/mm³ indicates neutropenia (normal WBC: 5,000-10,000/mm³). Chemotherapy-induced neutropenia significantly increases infection risk. The nurse should implement neutropenic precautions: private room, no fresh flowers or raw fruits/vegetables, strict hand hygiene, avoid invasive procedures, and monitor temperature closely. A hemoglobin of 10.2 g/dL is mildly low but not critical. Platelets at 140,000 are slightly low but not at bleeding risk level. Hematocrit 36% is within acceptable range. Source: Nurseslabs — Neutropenia Nursing Care; RegisteredNurseRN — Oncology Nursing.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client with suspected hypothyroidism. Which set of thyroid panel results is consistent with primary hypothyroidism?

options.text: TSH elevated, T4 decreased
TSH decreased, T4 elevated
TSH decreased, T4 decreased
TSH normal, T4 elevated

rationale: In primary hypothyroidism, the thyroid gland is not producing enough thyroid hormone (T4), so TSH is elevated as the pituitary gland attempts to stimulate the thyroid. This is the hallmark of primary hypothyroidism: high TSH + low T4. Low TSH with high T4 indicates hyperthyroidism. Low TSH with low T4 suggests secondary (pituitary) hypothyroidism. Normal TSH with elevated T4 is not a typical pattern for thyroid dysfunction. Source: RegisteredNurseRN — Thyroid Disorders; Nurseslabs — Endocrine Disorders.

stem: A nurse is reviewing the liver function tests of a client admitted with suspected hepatitis. Which combination of results is most indicative of acute hepatocellular damage?

options.text: Elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP) with normal ALT
Significantly elevated AST and ALT with elevated total bilirubin
Normal AST with decreased albumin only
Elevated BUN and creatinine with normal AST

rationale: In acute hepatocellular damage (such as hepatitis), AST and ALT are the primary markers that become significantly elevated because they are enzymes released from damaged liver cells. Elevated total bilirubin indicates the liver's impaired ability to conjugate and excrete bilirubin, causing jaundice. Elevated ALP with normal ALT suggests obstructive (cholestatic) rather than hepatocellular disease. Decreased albumin alone suggests chronic liver disease. Elevated BUN and creatinine indicate renal, not hepatic, dysfunction. Source: Nurseslabs — Liver Function Tests; RNpedia — Hepatic Disorders.

stem: A client presents to the emergency department with chest pain. The troponin I level drawn on admission is 0.02 ng/mL (normal: <0.04 ng/mL). A repeat troponin drawn 6 hours later is 2.8 ng/mL. How should the nurse interpret these results?

options.text: The results are normal and the client can be discharged
The rising troponin indicates acute myocardial injury and the nurse should anticipate cardiac interventions
The initial normal result rules out myocardial infarction
The elevated result is likely a lab error and should be redrawn

rationale: Troponin is the most specific cardiac biomarker for myocardial injury. Troponin levels may be normal immediately after a cardiac event and rise over 3-6 hours. A significant rise from normal (0.02) to markedly elevated (2.8) over 6 hours strongly indicates acute myocardial infarction (MI). Serial troponin measurements are essential because a single normal result does NOT rule out MI. The nurse should anticipate cardiac catheterization, thrombolytics, or other interventions. Assuming lab error with such a significant rise is inappropriate. Source: RegisteredNurseRN — Cardiac Markers; Nurseslabs — Acute Coronary Syndrome.

stem: A nurse is monitoring a client receiving IV heparin therapy. The aPTT result is 120 seconds (therapeutic range: 60-80 seconds). Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Stop the heparin infusion immediately
Notify the healthcare provider of the result
Assess the client for signs of bleeding
Double the infusion rate to reach therapeutic range
Have protamine sulfate readily available

rationale: An aPTT of 120 seconds is critically elevated (well above the therapeutic range of 60-80 seconds), indicating a high risk for hemorrhage. The nurse should: stop the heparin infusion to prevent further anticoagulation; notify the provider for orders; assess for bleeding (hematuria, melena, petechiae, gum bleeding, neurological changes); and have protamine sulfate (heparin antidote) available. Doubling the infusion rate is absolutely incorrect — the client is already over-anticoagulated. The aPTT should be 1.5-2.5 times the control value for therapeutic anticoagulation. Source: Nurseslabs — Heparin Therapy Nursing; RegisteredNurseRN — Anticoagulant Therapy.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client who is 4 hours post-abdominal surgery. Which finding is the earliest sign of post-operative hemorrhage?

options.text: Blood pressure of 80/50 mmHg
Increasing restlessness and anxiety
Hemoglobin of 6.0 g/dL
Urine output of 10 mL/hr

rationale: Increasing restlessness and anxiety are the earliest signs of hemorrhage and hypovolemic shock because the brain is very sensitive to decreased oxygen delivery. As blood volume decreases, the body initially compensates with increased heart rate and vasoconstriction, maintaining blood pressure temporarily. Hypotension (80/50 mmHg) is a late sign indicating decompensation. A critically low hemoglobin and decreased urine output are also later findings. Early recognition of hemorrhage allows for prompt intervention. Source: Nurseslabs — Post-Operative Complications; RegisteredNurseRN — Hypovolemic Shock.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client who had a total hip replacement 12 hours ago. Which intervention is most important for preventing deep vein thrombosis (DVT)?

options.text: Encouraging deep breathing exercises every 2 hours
Applying sequential compression devices (SCDs) as prescribed
Restricting fluid intake to reduce edema
Keeping the legs in a dependent position

rationale: Sequential compression devices (SCDs) are a primary mechanical intervention for DVT prevention in post-operative clients, especially after orthopedic surgery. SCDs promote venous return by intermittently compressing the legs, counteracting venous stasis — one of Virchow's triad factors (stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability). Deep breathing helps prevent pulmonary complications but is not the primary DVT intervention. Restricting fluids would increase viscosity and DVT risk. Dependent positioning promotes stasis and increases DVT risk — legs should be elevated. Source: Nurseslabs — DVT Prevention; RegisteredNurseRN — Venous Thromboembolism.

stem: A nurse is assessing a client who suddenly develops sharp chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia, and a sense of impending doom. The client had surgery 3 days ago and has been on bedrest. Which condition should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Myocardial infarction
Pulmonary embolism
Pneumothorax
Atelectasis

rationale: The clinical picture — sudden sharp chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia, and sense of impending doom in a post-operative client on bedrest — is classic for pulmonary embolism (PE). Surgery and immobility are major risk factors for DVT, which can dislodge and travel to the lungs. While MI can cause chest pain, the post-surgical bedrest history and sudden onset with dyspnea strongly suggest PE. Pneumothorax would present with absent breath sounds on one side. Atelectasis causes gradual-onset symptoms, not sudden sharp chest pain with a sense of impending doom. Source: Nurseslabs — Pulmonary Embolism; RegisteredNurseRN — PE Nursing Care.

stem: A nurse is assessing a client with a long leg cast applied 6 hours ago for a tibial fracture. The client reports severe, unrelenting pain in the lower leg that is not relieved by prescribed analgesics, and pain increases with passive extension of the toes. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Administer a higher dose of prescribed pain medication
Elevate the extremity above the level of the heart
Notify the healthcare provider immediately
Apply ice to the affected area and reassess in 30 minutes

rationale: The client is exhibiting classic signs of compartment syndrome: severe pain unrelieved by analgesics and pain with passive stretch of the muscles in the affected compartment. Compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency — the 5 P's are Pain (out of proportion), Pressure, Pallor, Pulselessness, and Paresthesia. The nurse must notify the provider immediately because a fasciotomy may be needed to prevent permanent tissue damage. Delaying for more pain medication, elevation (which may further decrease perfusion), or watchful waiting could result in irreversible neurovascular damage. Source: Nurseslabs — Compartment Syndrome; RegisteredNurseRN — Musculoskeletal Emergencies.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client who develops a tension pneumothorax after a central line insertion. Which assessment findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tracheal deviation toward the unaffected side
Absent breath sounds on the affected side
Bilateral crackles in the lung bases
Distended neck veins (JVD)
Hypotension and tachycardia

rationale: Tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening emergency where air enters the pleural space but cannot escape, causing increasing pressure that shifts mediastinal structures. Classic findings include: tracheal deviation away from the affected side (mediastinal shift), absent breath sounds on the affected side (collapsed lung), jugular venous distension (JVD) from impaired venous return, and hypotension with tachycardia (obstructive shock). Bilateral crackles suggest pulmonary edema or fluid overload, not pneumothorax. Immediate treatment is needle decompression followed by chest tube insertion. Source: Nurseslabs — Pneumothorax; RegisteredNurseRN — Tension Pneumothorax.

stem: A nurse enters a client's room and finds the client's abdominal surgical incision has dehisced with intestinal contents visible. What is the nurse's first action?

options.text: Push the intestinal contents back into the abdominal cavity
Cover the wound with sterile saline-moistened dressings
Apply a dry sterile dressing and tape securely
Position the client in high Fowler's position

rationale: When wound evisceration occurs (organs protruding through the wound), the nurse should immediately cover the exposed organs with sterile saline-moistened dressings to prevent drying, infection, and tissue damage. Never attempt to push organs back into the abdominal cavity as this can cause tissue damage and contamination. Dry dressings would adhere to and damage the exposed tissue. The client should be placed in low Fowler's position (15-20 degrees) with knees bent to reduce abdominal tension — not high Fowler's. The nurse should then notify the surgeon immediately for emergency surgical repair. Source: Nurseslabs — Wound Dehiscence and Evisceration; RNpedia — Post-Operative Complications.

stem: A nurse is planning care for a client with dysphagia following a stroke. Which intervention is most important to prevent aspiration?

options.text: Place the client in a supine position during meals
Offer thin liquids to make swallowing easier
Position the client upright at 90 degrees and thicken liquids as prescribed
Encourage the client to use a straw for all drinks

rationale: For clients with dysphagia, the most important aspiration prevention measures are: positioning the client upright (high Fowler's, 90 degrees) during and for 30 minutes after meals, and thickening liquids as prescribed by the speech therapist. Upright positioning uses gravity to direct food into the esophagus. Supine positioning greatly increases aspiration risk. Thin liquids are the most difficult to swallow safely for clients with dysphagia — they move too quickly and can enter the airway. Straws increase the speed of liquid flow and aspiration risk. The client should also tilt the chin down (chin tuck) while swallowing and eat small bites. Source: RegisteredNurseRN — Dysphagia Nursing Care; Nurseslabs — Stroke Nursing Interventions.

stem: A nurse is assessing a client in the post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) after general anesthesia. Which findings indicate the client is ready for discharge from the PACU? Select all that apply.

options.text: The client is able to move all four extremities voluntarily
Oxygen saturation is maintained above 94% on room air
The client's blood pressure is within 20% of the preoperative baseline
The client remains unconscious but has stable vital signs
The client is awake and oriented or at preoperative level of consciousness

rationale: PACU discharge readiness is assessed using the Aldrete scoring system, which evaluates: activity (ability to move extremities), respiration (adequate SpO2), circulation (blood pressure within 20% of baseline), consciousness (awake and oriented), and oxygen saturation (>92% on room air). A client who is unconscious is not ready for discharge regardless of vital sign stability — consciousness is a key criterion. All other options describe criteria that must be met for safe PACU discharge. The total Aldrete score should be 9-10 (out of 10) for discharge. Source: Nurseslabs — PACU Nursing Care; RegisteredNurseRN — Post-Anesthesia Recovery.

stem: A nurse is monitoring the fetal heart rate tracing of a laboring client. The tracing shows the fetal heart rate decreasing after the peak of each contraction and returning to baseline after the contraction ends. Which type of deceleration is this, and what does it indicate?

options.text: Early decelerations — caused by head compression; reassuring pattern
Late decelerations — caused by uteroplacental insufficiency; non-reassuring pattern
Variable decelerations — caused by cord compression; requires repositioning
Prolonged decelerations — caused by cord prolapse; emergency delivery needed

rationale: Late decelerations begin after the peak of a contraction and return to baseline after the contraction ends — the nadir is offset from the contraction peak. They indicate uteroplacental insufficiency (inadequate oxygen delivery to the fetus) and are a non-reassuring pattern requiring intervention: left lateral positioning, IV fluids, oxygen, stop oxytocin if infusing, and notify the provider. Early decelerations mirror contractions (onset and offset with contraction) and are caused by fetal head compression — they are benign. Variable decelerations have an abrupt onset and variable timing relative to contractions, caused by cord compression. Source: RegisteredNurseRN — Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring; Nurseslabs — Fetal Monitoring.

stem: A nurse is monitoring a client's central venous pressure (CVP). The reading is 12 mmHg. Which condition should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Hypovolemia
Fluid volume overload
Normal fluid balance
Cardiac tamponade has been resolved

rationale: Normal CVP is 2-8 mmHg (or 3-8 cm H₂O). A CVP of 12 mmHg is elevated and indicates increased right atrial pressure, commonly caused by fluid volume overload, right-sided heart failure, cardiac tamponade, or pulmonary hypertension. A low CVP (<2 mmHg) would suggest hypovolemia. The nurse should assess for other signs of fluid overload: crackles, edema, weight gain, and distended neck veins. Interventions may include fluid restriction and diuretics as prescribed. Source: Nurseslabs — CVP Monitoring; RegisteredNurseRN — Hemodynamic Monitoring.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client with an arterial line in the radial artery. The waveform appears dampened with a flattened tracing. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Remove the arterial line and replace it in the other arm
Check the tubing for air bubbles, kinks, or blood clots
Increase the IV fluid rate to raise the blood pressure
Obtain a cuff blood pressure and document the dampened reading as accurate

rationale: A dampened arterial line waveform (flattened, with reduced systolic and elevated diastolic readings) is most commonly caused by a mechanical issue: air bubbles in the tubing, kinked tubing, a loose connection, or a clot at the catheter tip. The nurse should first troubleshoot by checking the system for these issues, flushing the line per protocol, and ensuring proper leveling. Removing the line is premature without troubleshooting. Increasing IV fluids addresses blood pressure, not the waveform issue. Accepting a dampened reading as accurate would lead to clinical decisions based on unreliable data. Source: Nurseslabs — Arterial Line Nursing Care; RNpedia — Hemodynamic Monitoring.

stem: A nurse is monitoring a client after a thoracentesis. Which assessment finding requires immediate intervention?

options.text: Mild discomfort at the puncture site
Absent breath sounds on the affected side with increasing dyspnea
Small amount of serous drainage on the dressing
Respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute

rationale: Absent breath sounds on the affected side with increasing dyspnea after thoracentesis indicates a pneumothorax — the most serious complication of this procedure. The needle may have punctured the visceral pleura, allowing air into the pleural space and causing lung collapse. The nurse should immediately notify the provider, prepare for chest X-ray and possible chest tube insertion, and provide oxygen. Mild site discomfort is expected. A small amount of serous drainage is normal. A respiratory rate of 18 is normal. Post-thoracentesis nursing includes vital signs every 15 minutes for 1 hour and bilateral breath sound assessment. Source: Nurseslabs — Thoracentesis Nursing Care; RegisteredNurseRN — Respiratory Procedures.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client who had a paracentesis with 3 liters of ascitic fluid removed. Which complication should the nurse monitor for most closely in the first few hours?

options.text: Hypervolemia and pulmonary edema
Hypotension and tachycardia due to fluid shift
Hypertension and bradycardia
Hyperglycemia from stress response

rationale: After large-volume paracentesis, the most significant immediate complication is hypotension due to fluid shifting from the intravascular space into the peritoneal cavity to replace the removed fluid (third-spacing). Removal of large volumes (>1-2 liters) can cause hypovolemia, manifesting as hypotension and compensatory tachycardia. The nurse should monitor vital signs frequently, measure abdominal girth, weigh the client, and administer IV albumin as prescribed to maintain intravascular volume. The client would not develop hypervolemia since fluid was removed. Hypertension would not be expected. Source: Nurseslabs — Paracentesis Nursing Care; RegisteredNurseRN — Liver Cirrhosis Nursing.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client receiving peritoneal dialysis. During the drain cycle, the client reports abdominal pain and the effluent appears cloudy. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Continue the dialysis and monitor the effluent for clearing
Obtain a sample of the effluent for culture and notify the provider
Increase the dwell time to improve dialysis efficiency
Warm the dialysate solution and continue exchanges

rationale: Cloudy effluent with abdominal pain during peritoneal dialysis is the hallmark sign of peritonitis, the most serious and common complication. The nurse should immediately obtain an effluent sample for culture and sensitivity testing and notify the provider. Peritonitis requires prompt antibiotic treatment — delay can lead to sepsis. Normal effluent should be clear or pale yellow. Continuing dialysis without investigating, increasing dwell time, or warming the solution are all inappropriate responses to signs of infection. Other signs of peritonitis include fever, rebound tenderness, and nausea/vomiting. Source: Nurseslabs — Peritoneal Dialysis Nursing; RegisteredNurseRN — Renal Failure Nursing.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client with an arteriovenous (AV) fistula in the left arm who is receiving hemodialysis. Which assessment finding requires immediate action?

options.text: A palpable thrill over the fistula site
An audible bruit on auscultation of the fistula
Absence of thrill and bruit over the fistula
Mild swelling of the left hand after dialysis treatment

rationale: Absence of a thrill (palpable vibration) and bruit (audible rushing sound) over an AV fistula indicates fistula thrombosis or occlusion — a medical emergency requiring immediate intervention to restore blood flow. A functioning AV fistula should always have a palpable thrill and audible bruit, indicating adequate blood flow. The nurse should notify the provider immediately. A thrill and bruit are normal, expected findings. Mild hand swelling may occur but is not an emergency. Nursing care for AV fistulas includes: no blood pressures, no venipunctures, and no tourniquets on the affected arm. Source: Nurseslabs — Hemodialysis Nursing Care; RegisteredNurseRN — Vascular Access.

stem: A nurse is assessing a client using the Glasgow Coma Scale. The client opens eyes to verbal stimulation (3), responds with incomprehensible sounds (2), and has flexion withdrawal to pain (4). Calculate the client's GCS score.
rationale: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) has three components: Eye opening (1-4), Verbal response (1-5), and Motor response (1-6). This client scores: Eye opening to verbal stimulation = 3, Verbal with incomprehensible sounds = 2, Motor with flexion withdrawal = 4. Total GCS = 3 + 2 + 4 = 9. GCS ranges from 3 (deep coma) to 15 (fully alert). A score of 8 or below generally indicates severe brain injury and need for intubation. This client at GCS 9 is in moderate brain injury range (9-12) and requires close monitoring. Source: Nurseslabs — Glasgow Coma Scale; RegisteredNurseRN — Neurological Assessment.

stem: A client presents to the emergency department with crushing substernal chest pain radiating to the left arm, diaphoresis, and nausea. The 12-lead ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Which type of myocardial infarction should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Anterior wall MI
Lateral wall MI
Inferior wall MI
Septal MI

rationale: ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF indicates an inferior wall STEMI (ST-elevation myocardial infarction), involving the right coronary artery territory. Anterior wall MI shows changes in V1-V4 (LAD artery). Lateral wall MI shows changes in leads I, aVL, V5-V6 (circumflex artery). Septal MI shows changes in V1-V2. For inferior MI, the nurse should also assess for right ventricular involvement (right-sided ECG leads) and avoid nitrates if right ventricular MI is suspected due to preload dependence. Source: RegisteredNurseRN — Myocardial Infarction; Nurseslabs — Acute Coronary Syndrome.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client who had cardiac surgery and develops muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins, and hypotension. Which condition should the nurse suspect, and what is the priority intervention?

options.text: Heart failure; administer diuretics
Cardiac tamponade; prepare for pericardiocentesis
Tension pneumothorax; prepare for needle decompression
Myocardial infarction; administer thrombolytics

rationale: Beck's triad — muffled (distant) heart sounds, jugular venous distension (JVD), and hypotension — is the classic presentation of cardiac tamponade, where fluid accumulates in the pericardial sac and compresses the heart, impairing filling. The priority intervention is pericardiocentesis (needle aspiration of pericardial fluid). Cardiac tamponade is common after cardiac surgery due to post-operative bleeding. Heart failure would present with crackles and edema. Tension pneumothorax presents with tracheal deviation and absent breath sounds. MI would not cause muffled heart sounds. Source: Nurseslabs — Cardiac Tamponade; RegisteredNurseRN — Pericardial Disorders.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client with new-onset atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 150 bpm. The client reports feeling dizzy and lightheaded. Which intervention should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Administer atropine 0.5 mg IV push
Prepare for synchronized cardioversion
Perform vagal maneuvers
Administer adenosine rapid IV push

rationale: A client with atrial fibrillation at a rapid ventricular rate (150 bpm) who is symptomatic (dizzy, lightheaded — hemodynamically unstable) requires synchronized cardioversion as the priority intervention. Atropine is used for bradycardia, not tachycardia. Vagal maneuvers and adenosine are used for supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), not atrial fibrillation. If the client were hemodynamically stable, rate control medications (diltiazem, beta-blockers, or amiodarone) would be used first. Anticoagulation is also a key consideration for A-fib due to stroke risk. Source: RegisteredNurseRN — Atrial Fibrillation; Nurseslabs — Cardiac Arrhythmias.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client in the ICU who develops a blood pressure of 70/40 mmHg, tachycardia, cold/clammy skin, elevated CVP, and distended neck veins. Which type of shock should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Hypovolemic shock
Septic shock (warm phase)
Cardiogenic shock
Neurogenic shock

rationale: Cardiogenic shock is characterized by hypotension, tachycardia, cold/clammy skin (vasoconstriction), elevated CVP, and JVD — indicating the heart is failing as a pump and blood is backing up. The elevated CVP and JVD differentiate it from hypovolemic shock (which has low CVP). Septic shock warm phase presents with warm, flushed skin and vasodilation. Neurogenic shock presents with bradycardia (loss of sympathetic tone) and warm skin. Cardiogenic shock is treated with inotropes (dobutamine), vasopressors, and possibly an intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP). Source: Nurseslabs — Cardiogenic Shock; RegisteredNurseRN — Types of Shock.

stem: A nurse is assessing a client with infective endocarditis. Which finding is characteristic of this condition?

options.text: Pericardial friction rub with sharp chest pain
New-onset heart murmur with Janeway lesions on the palms
Sudden onset of severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back
Bilateral pitting edema with nocturnal dyspnea

rationale: Infective endocarditis involves infection of the heart valves, presenting with a new or changing heart murmur (from valve damage) and peripheral manifestations: Janeway lesions (painless erythematous lesions on palms/soles), Osler nodes (painful nodules on fingers/toes), splinter hemorrhages (nail bed), and Roth spots (retinal hemorrhages). Pericardial friction rub with chest pain indicates pericarditis. Tearing chest pain to the back suggests aortic dissection. Bilateral edema with dyspnea suggests heart failure. Blood cultures (3 sets from different sites) are essential for diagnosis. Source: Nurseslabs — Infective Endocarditis; RegisteredNurseRN — Endocarditis Nursing.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client with status asthmaticus who is not responding to repeated nebulizer treatments. The client's oxygen saturation is 85% and they are using accessory muscles to breathe. Which intervention is the highest priority?

options.text: Administer another albuterol nebulizer treatment
Prepare for endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation
Encourage the client to use a peak flow meter
Administer a leukotriene modifier orally

rationale: Status asthmaticus is a severe, life-threatening asthma attack that does not respond to conventional bronchodilator therapy. With an SpO2 of 85% and accessory muscle use despite repeated treatments, the client is in respiratory failure and requires intubation and mechanical ventilation as the priority. Repeating nebulizers that have already failed is ineffective. A peak flow meter is inappropriate in acute respiratory distress. Oral leukotriene modifiers are for maintenance therapy, not acute emergencies. IV corticosteroids, IV magnesium sulfate, and epinephrine may also be used. Source: RegisteredNurseRN — Status Asthmaticus; Nurseslabs — Asthma Nursing Management.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client diagnosed with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Which assessment findings are characteristic of this condition? Select all that apply.

options.text: Refractory hypoxemia not responsive to supplemental oxygen
Bilateral white-out infiltrates on chest X-ray
PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio less than 300 mmHg
Elevated pulmonary artery wedge pressure indicating cardiac cause
Progressive dyspnea and tachypnea

rationale: ARDS is characterized by: refractory hypoxemia (the hallmark — PaO₂ does not improve adequately with increasing FiO₂), bilateral diffuse infiltrates on chest X-ray ("white-out" or "ground glass" appearance), a PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio <300 (mild ARDS <300, moderate <200, severe <100), and progressive respiratory distress with tachypnea. ARDS is non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema — the PAWP should be <18 mmHg (elevated PAWP indicates cardiogenic pulmonary edema). Management includes mechanical ventilation with low tidal volumes (6 mL/kg), PEEP, prone positioning, and treating the underlying cause. Source: Nurseslabs — ARDS Nursing Care; RegisteredNurseRN — ARDS Review.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client with acute pulmonary edema. The client is sitting upright, is severely dyspneic with pink frothy sputum, and has crackles throughout both lung fields. Which medication should the nurse administer first?

options.text: Furosemide (Lasix) IV as prescribed
Oral potassium chloride supplement
Metoprolol (Lopressor) oral dose
Lisinopril (Zestril) oral dose

rationale: Acute (flash) pulmonary edema with pink frothy sputum indicates severe fluid overload in the lungs. The priority medication is IV furosemide (loop diuretic) to rapidly reduce fluid volume and preload. The classic mnemonic for acute pulmonary edema treatment is LMNOP: Lasix (furosemide), Morphine, Nitrates, Oxygen, Position (high Fowler's). Oral potassium is a supplement, not an emergency drug. Metoprolol (beta-blocker) and lisinopril (ACE inhibitor) are maintenance medications and work too slowly for acute management. High-flow oxygen and IV nitroglycerin may also be administered. Source: RegisteredNurseRN — Pulmonary Edema; Nurseslabs — Heart Failure Nursing.

stem: A nurse is caring for a trauma client who develops a tension pneumothorax. While awaiting the provider, which position should the nurse place the client in?

options.text: Supine with legs elevated (Trendelenburg)
High Fowler's position on the affected side
Semi-Fowler's to high Fowler's position
Prone position

rationale: For tension pneumothorax, the client should be positioned in semi-Fowler's to high Fowler's position to facilitate breathing and reduce respiratory distress. This position uses gravity to lower the diaphragm and maximize lung expansion of the unaffected lung. Trendelenburg would worsen respiratory distress by pushing abdominal contents against the diaphragm. Lying on the affected side may compromise the unaffected lung. Prone positioning is inappropriate for an acute emergency. Definitive treatment is needle decompression at the second intercostal space, midclavicular line, followed by chest tube insertion. Source: Nurseslabs — Pneumothorax; RegisteredNurseRN — Chest Trauma.

stem: A nurse is assessing a client with respiratory failure. The arterial blood gas results show: pH 7.22, PaCO₂ 68 mmHg, PaO₂ 52 mmHg, HCO₃ 24 mEq/L. Which type of respiratory failure does this represent?

options.text: Type I (hypoxemic) respiratory failure
Type II (hypercapnic) respiratory failure
Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
Mixed respiratory and metabolic alkalosis

rationale: The ABG shows: acidotic pH (7.22), elevated PaCO₂ (68 mmHg — normal 35-45), low PaO₂ (52 mmHg), and normal HCO₃ (24 mEq/L). This is uncompensated respiratory acidosis consistent with Type II (hypercapnic/ventilatory) respiratory failure — the client cannot adequately ventilate to remove CO₂. Common causes include COPD exacerbation, respiratory muscle fatigue, and CNS depression. Type I (hypoxemic) failure shows low PaO₂ with normal or low PaCO₂ (e.g., pneumonia, ARDS). Metabolic acidosis would show low HCO₃. Treatment includes bronchodilators, non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP), or intubation. Source: RegisteredNurseRN — ABG Interpretation; Nurseslabs — Respiratory Failure.

stem: A client arrives at the emergency department with sudden onset of right-sided weakness, slurred speech, and facial drooping that started 45 minutes ago. After confirming an ischemic stroke on CT scan, which intervention is the highest priority?

options.text: Administer IV alteplase (tPA) within the treatment window
Administer aspirin 325 mg orally immediately
Perform a carotid endarterectomy
Start IV heparin infusion for anticoagulation

rationale: For confirmed ischemic stroke within the treatment window (up to 4.5 hours from symptom onset), IV alteplase (tPA) is the priority intervention — it dissolves the clot and restores blood flow. This client is within the window at 45 minutes. Aspirin is given but not within 24 hours of tPA administration. Carotid endarterectomy is a surgical preventive measure, not an acute treatment. IV heparin is contraindicated acutely with tPA and is not first-line for ischemic stroke. Key nursing actions: monitor neuro status every 15 minutes, maintain BP parameters, and assess for bleeding complications. Source: Nurseslabs — Ischemic Stroke; RegisteredNurseRN — Stroke Nursing Care.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client with a seizure disorder who has been seizing continuously for 8 minutes without regaining consciousness between seizures. Which medication should the nurse anticipate administering first?

options.text: Phenytoin (Dilantin) IV loading dose
Lorazepam (Ativan) IV
Valproic acid (Depakote) orally
Carbamazepine (Tegretol) orally

rationale: Status epilepticus is defined as continuous seizure activity lasting >5 minutes or two or more seizures without regaining consciousness. The first-line treatment is a benzodiazepine — lorazepam (Ativan) IV is the preferred initial drug to rapidly stop seizure activity. If benzodiazepines fail, second-line agents include IV phenytoin (fosphenytoin), levetiracetam, or valproic acid. Oral medications cannot be given during active seizures. The nurse should protect the client from injury, maintain airway, position on side, time the seizure, and never restrain or insert objects in the mouth. Source: RegisteredNurseRN — Status Epilepticus; Nurseslabs — Seizure Nursing Management.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client with a spinal cord injury at T4. The client suddenly develops a severe pounding headache, blood pressure of 240/140 mmHg, profuse sweating above the injury level, and bradycardia. Which action should the nurse perform first?

options.text: Administer prescribed antihypertensive medication
Sit the client upright and check for a distended bladder
Place the client flat and prepare for IV fluid bolus
Apply a cold compress to the forehead and continue monitoring

rationale: This is autonomic dysreflexia — a life-threatening emergency in clients with spinal cord injuries at T6 or above. The most common trigger is bladder distension. The first action is to sit the client upright (to lower BP using orthostatic effect) and identify/remove the noxious stimulus — check for full bladder (catheterize if needed), fecal impaction, tight clothing, or skin irritation. Antihypertensives may be needed but addressing the cause is the priority first action. Placing the client flat would worsen the dangerously high BP. Cold compresses do not address the underlying emergency. If untreated, the extreme hypertension can cause stroke, seizures, or death. Source: Nurseslabs — Autonomic Dysreflexia; RegisteredNurseRN — Spinal Cord Injury.

stem: A nurse is assessing a client suspected of having bacterial meningitis. Which assessment findings are most consistent with this diagnosis?

options.text: Fever, nuchal rigidity, and positive Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs
Low-grade fever, clear nasal drainage, and photophobia
Afebrile with unilateral facial weakness and hearing loss
Headache with visual field deficits and papilledema

rationale: The classic triad of bacterial meningitis is: fever, nuchal rigidity (stiff neck), and altered mental status. Positive Kernig's sign (pain with leg extension when hip is flexed) and Brudzinski's sign (involuntary hip/knee flexion when neck is flexed) indicate meningeal irritation. Photophobia and severe headache are also common. Droplet precautions are required for the first 24 hours of antibiotic therapy. Unilateral facial weakness suggests Bell's palsy or stroke. Visual field deficits with papilledema suggest increased intracranial pressure from a mass lesion. A lumbar puncture is needed for definitive diagnosis. Source: RegisteredNurseRN — Meningitis; Nurseslabs — Meningitis Nursing Care.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client with Graves' disease who develops a temperature of 104°F (40°C), heart rate of 160 bpm, agitation, and delirium. Which life-threatening complication should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Myxedema coma
Thyroid storm (thyrotoxic crisis)
Addisonian crisis
Pheochromocytoma crisis

rationale: Thyroid storm (thyrotoxic crisis) is a life-threatening exacerbation of hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease) characterized by severe hyperthermia (>104°F), extreme tachycardia, agitation/delirium, and potential cardiovascular collapse. Treatment includes: PTU or methimazole (block thyroid hormone synthesis), beta-blockers (control heart rate), corticosteroids (block T4 to T3 conversion), cooling measures, and IV fluids. Myxedema coma is the opposite — severe hypothyroidism with hypothermia and bradycardia. Addisonian crisis involves cortisol deficiency with hypotension. Pheochromocytoma causes episodic hypertension but not sustained high fever. Source: Nurseslabs — Thyroid Storm; RegisteredNurseRN — Hyperthyroidism.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client with severe hypothyroidism who becomes increasingly lethargic with a temperature of 93°F (33.9°C), bradycardia, and hypotension. Which emergency condition should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Thyroid storm
Myxedema coma
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state

rationale: Myxedema coma is the most severe, life-threatening form of hypothyroidism characterized by: hypothermia, altered mental status progressing to coma, bradycardia, hypotension, hypoventilation, and hypoglycemia. It is a medical emergency requiring IV levothyroxine (T4), IV corticosteroids, passive warming (avoid active warming — can cause vasodilation and cardiovascular collapse), respiratory support, and glucose management. Thyroid storm is the opposite — hyperthyroidism crisis with hyperthermia and tachycardia. DKA and HHS are diabetic emergencies with hyperglycemia. Source: RegisteredNurseRN — Myxedema Coma; Nurseslabs — Hypothyroidism.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client with Addison's disease who develops sudden severe hypotension, tachycardia, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain after abruptly discontinuing corticosteroid therapy. Which intervention is the priority?

options.text: Administer IV hydrocortisone (Solu-Cortef) and IV fluids with dextrose
Administer oral prednisone and monitor blood pressure
Restrict fluid intake and administer vasopressors
Administer insulin to correct metabolic imbalances

rationale: Addisonian crisis (acute adrenal insufficiency) is triggered by abrupt corticosteroid withdrawal, stress, infection, or trauma in a client with adrenal insufficiency. It presents with severe hypotension, tachycardia, dehydration, hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, and hypoglycemia. The priority is IV hydrocortisone (stress-dose steroids) and aggressive IV fluid resuscitation with dextrose-containing solutions (to correct dehydration and hypoglycemia). Oral medications are inadequate in a crisis — IV is essential. Fluid restriction would worsen dehydration. Insulin is not indicated — the client has hypoglycemia, not hyperglycemia. This is why corticosteroids must always be tapered, never stopped abruptly. Source: Nurseslabs — Addisonian Crisis; RegisteredNurseRN — Adrenal Insufficiency.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client with type 2 diabetes who presents with blood glucose of 820 mg/dL, serum osmolality of 350 mOsm/kg, minimal urine ketones, and profound dehydration. Which condition should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS)
Hypoglycemic shock
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH)

rationale: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) is characterized by: extreme hyperglycemia (often >600 mg/dL), hyperosmolality (>320 mOsm/kg), profound dehydration, and minimal or no ketones (because the client still produces some insulin). HHS typically occurs in type 2 diabetes. DKA shows moderate hyperglycemia (250-500 mg/dL), significant ketones, and metabolic acidosis — it occurs in type 1 diabetes. Hypoglycemic shock involves low blood glucose. SIADH involves fluid retention and dilutional hyponatremia. Treatment of HHS focuses on aggressive IV fluid replacement (isotonic saline) and insulin infusion. Source: RegisteredNurseRN — HHS vs DKA; Nurseslabs — Diabetic Emergencies.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client diagnosed with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Which assessment findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.

options.text: Oozing blood from IV sites and puncture wounds
Petechiae and purpura on the skin
Elevated platelet count and elevated fibrinogen
Prolonged PT, aPTT, and elevated D-dimer
Decreased platelet count and decreased fibrinogen

rationale: DIC is a paradoxical condition of simultaneous clotting and bleeding. As clotting factors and platelets are consumed in widespread microthrombi, the client develops bleeding: oozing from IV sites, petechiae, purpura, hematuria, and GI bleeding. Lab findings show: decreased platelets (consumed), decreased fibrinogen (consumed), prolonged PT/aPTT (depleted clotting factors), and elevated D-dimer/FDPs (fibrin degradation from clot breakdown). Elevated platelets and fibrinogen would indicate normal coagulation or inflammation, not DIC. Treatment focuses on the underlying cause plus replacement of clotting factors (FFP, cryoprecipitate) and platelets. Source: Nurseslabs — DIC; RegisteredNurseRN — Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client with suspected sepsis. Place the following nursing interventions in the correct order of priority according to the Surviving Sepsis Campaign bundle.

options.text: Obtain blood cultures before starting antibiotics
Measure serum lactate level
Administer broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour
Begin IV crystalloid fluid bolus (30 mL/kg) for hypotension
Reassess volume status and tissue perfusion

rationale: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign 1-hour bundle requires: (1) Measure lactate — establishes severity (lactate >2 mmol/L indicates tissue hypoperfusion); (2) Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics — allows identification of causative organism without delaying treatment; (3) Administer broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour of recognition — every hour of delay increases mortality; (4) Begin rapid IV fluid resuscitation (30 mL/kg crystalloid) for hypotension or lactate ≥4 — restores intravascular volume; (5) Reassess volume status — guide further fluid or vasopressor therapy. SIRS criteria include: temp >38°C or <36°C, HR >90, RR >20, WBC >12,000 or <4,000. Source: Nurseslabs — Sepsis Nursing; RegisteredNurseRN — Sepsis and SIRS.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client admitted with severe burns covering 36% of the total body surface area. Using the Parkland formula, how much IV lactated Ringer's solution should be administered in the first 8 hours for a client weighing 80 kg?
rationale: The Parkland formula for burn fluid resuscitation is: 4 mL × body weight (kg) × %TBSA burned. Total 24-hour volume = 4 × 80 × 36 = 11,520 mL. Half of this total is given in the first 8 hours from the time of burn injury: 11,520 ÷ 2 = 5,760 mL. The remaining half is given over the next 16 hours. Lactated Ringer's is the preferred crystalloid. Urine output (0.5-1 mL/kg/hr in adults) is the best indicator of adequate resuscitation. The Rule of Nines is used to estimate TBSA: each arm 9%, each leg 18%, anterior trunk 18%, posterior trunk 18%, head 9%, perineum 1%. Source: Nurseslabs — Burns Nursing Care; RegisteredNurseRN — Burn Management.

stem: A nurse is caring for a client with sickle cell disease who presents with severe bone pain, fever, and swelling of the joints. Which priority intervention should the nurse implement?

options.text: Apply cold packs to the painful areas
Administer IV fluids and pain management as prescribed
Restrict fluids to prevent fluid overload
Encourage vigorous physical activity to promote circulation

rationale: During a sickle cell crisis (vaso-occlusive crisis), sickled red blood cells block small blood vessels, causing severe ischemic pain. Priority interventions include: aggressive IV hydration (to dilute blood and promote flow of sickled cells), effective pain management (often requiring opioids — pain is severe), oxygen therapy (to prevent further sickling), rest, and warmth. Cold packs are contraindicated — cold causes vasoconstriction and worsens sickling. Fluid restriction would worsen the crisis. Vigorous activity increases oxygen demand and can trigger more sickling. Source: RegisteredNurseRN — Sickle Cell Disease; Nurseslabs — Sickle Cell Anemia.

stem: A nurse is monitoring a client receiving chemotherapy who develops tumor lysis syndrome. Which electrolyte abnormality should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Hypokalemia and hypocalcemia
Hyperkalemia and hyperuricemia
Hyponatremia and hypoglycemia
Hypernatremia and hyperchloremia

rationale: Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) occurs when rapid destruction of cancer cells releases intracellular contents into the bloodstream. The classic electrolyte pattern is: hyperkalemia (potassium release from cells), hyperphosphatemia (phosphorus release), hypocalcemia (calcium binds to excess phosphorus), and hyperuricemia (nucleic acid breakdown). Acute kidney injury can develop from uric acid crystal deposition. Prevention includes aggressive IV hydration, allopurinol or rasburicase (to reduce uric acid), and monitoring electrolytes every 6-8 hours. Cardiac monitoring is essential due to hyperkalemia risk. Source: Nurseslabs — Tumor Lysis Syndrome; RegisteredNurseRN — Oncologic Emergencies.

stem: A nurse is assessing a client admitted with acute pancreatitis. Which is the most characteristic symptom the nurse should expect?

options.text: Sudden onset of sharp right lower quadrant pain
Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, worse after eating
Colicky pain with rebound tenderness in the left lower quadrant
Dull, constant right upper quadrant pain with jaundice

rationale: Acute pancreatitis classically presents with severe, steady epigastric pain radiating straight through to the back, worsened by eating (especially fatty foods) and lying flat. Pain may be partially relieved by leaning forward or assuming a fetal position. Other findings include elevated serum amylase and lipase (most specific), nausea/vomiting, and possible Cullen sign (periumbilical bruising) or Grey Turner sign (flank bruising) in severe hemorrhagic pancreatitis. RLQ pain suggests appendicitis. LLQ colicky pain suggests diverticulitis. RUQ pain with jaundice suggests cholecystitis or biliary obstruction. Management includes NPO, IV fluids, pain management, and NG tube if ileus develops. Source: Nurseslabs — Acute Pancreatitis; RegisteredNurseRN — Pancreatitis Nursing.
